question: Following the United States’ designation of the Cartel of the Suns as a terrorist organisation, Gustavo Petro’s government in Colombia has demonstrated its unwillingness to fight drug trafficking by denying that the cartel exists.

This comes at a time when Colombians are once again suffering as a result of violence and the killing of their compatriots, politicians and members of the security forces – something that had not occurred for decades.

Under the pretext of cooperation and the misnamed ‘peace process’ – one outcome of which has been the institutionalisation of terrorists in Colombia – the EU has poured millions of euros into promoting a non-existent ‘peace’ that has served only to support totalitarian forces, as we have seen in the wake of the terrible attacks and killings committed by organised crime groups. With the above in mind: 1.

Does the Vice-President / High Representative believe that the EU can continue to fund a government which, instead of combating transnational criminal organisations, appears to be helping to hide them?
Is an urgent overhaul of the EU’s cooperation and funding policy towards Colombia envisaged in this context?
What specific action is the EU intending to take to prevent European taxpayers’ money from ending up funding criminal groups?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.10.2025) The EU will continue to support Colombia in the common fight against drugs trafficking and organised crime. Colombia’s active participation in EU-funded programmes and its close cooperation with agencies like the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (EUROPOL) and the European Drugs Agency are of enormous value for the safety of Europe.

Inter alia, this collaboration enhances the capacities of security forces of both sides and facilitates police and judicial cooperation in the pursuit of criminals and terrorists. Examples of successes include the shutdown of Kidflix, one of world’s largest paedophile platforms, and the seizure of 1 400 tons of drugs by operation Orion.

Given the threat posed by organised crime, the EU will intensify its police and judicial cooperation with Colombia. The EU and Colombia aim to further improve the exchange of information between EUROPOL and Colombia, intensify cooperation in areas such as seizures at sea, trafficking of weapons, and the execution of mutual legal assistance and extradition requests.

The EU and Colombia are also negotiating a new agreement on judicial cooperation with European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation. The EU will also continue to support Colombian peace efforts, in recognition of the inextricable link between the pursuit of peace and the fight against crime in Colombia.
Regular monitoring, such as reports, evaluations and data collection efforts, ensure accountability of EU funds.
